title: A job as a tour guide

script.t: My guest today is Marco Bianchi, who works as a tour guide in Rome. Marco, how did you start?

Well, I studied history at university, and I always loved telling people stories about the past. After I finished, I couldn't find a job as a teacher, so a friend suggested I try guiding tourists for a summer. That was eleven years ago, and I'm still doing it!
What does a normal day look like?

In summer, I usually do two tours a day. The morning tour starts at eight, before it gets too hot, and we visit the Colosseum and the Forum. In the afternoon I often take a smaller group to the Vatican museums. I walk about fifteen kilometres a day, so I don't need to go to the gym!
What's the best part of the job?
Meeting people from all over the world. Last week I had a group of retired teachers from Japan who knew more about Roman emperors than I did! I learn something new almost every day.
And the worst part?
Probably the heat in July and August. And sometimes people are more interested in taking selfies than listening to the history. But I try to make the stories funny, so they pay attention.
What advice would you give someone who wants to do your job?
Learn languages. I speak English, Spanish and French, and that gives me many more opportunities. And practise speaking in front of people, because you need to be confident.

script.t: Have you decided what to study at university yet, Ella?
Not really. My parents want me to study medicine, because my grades in biology and chemistry are good. But I'm not sure I want to spend six years studying and then work at night in a hospital.
When do you have to decide?
By the end of March. And every time I think about it, I change my mind. It's driving me crazy.
What would you really like to do?
Honestly? Something with design. I love drawing, and I've been making little videos and posters for the school drama club. People say they're really good.
Then why not study graphic design?
I'm worried about finding a job afterwards. My cousin studied art and now she works in a supermarket.
But design is different. Every company needs websites and adverts. My brother works for a design agency and he's always saying they can't find enough good designers.
Really? Do you think he'd talk to me about it?
I'm sure he would. He's coming home next weekend. I'll ask him to call you.
That would be great. I also need to tell my parents what I'm thinking. They'll be disappointed.
Maybe not, if you explain it well. You could show them your work and some information about jobs.
That's a good idea. I'll prepare a little presentation. That's what designers do, isn't it?

title: Repair cafés
model: Cambridge B1 Preliminary – Listening Part 2/4 (radio feature)

script.t: Have you ever thrown away a toaster or a lamp just because one small part was broken? You're not alone. Every year, millions of electrical items end up in rubbish dumps, even though many of them could easily be fixed. That's why repair cafés are becoming so popular. The first repair café opened in Amsterdam in 2009. The idea was simple: once a month, volunteers with practical skills, like electricians, tailors and carpenters, meet in a community centre, and local people bring their broken things for them to repair. Today there are more than two thousand repair cafés around the world. At our local repair café, which meets on the first Saturday of every month in the church hall on Mill Road, the most common items are lamps, coffee machines and clothes. The volunteers manage to fix about seventy per cent of everything people bring. And the service is free, although visitors can leave a donation if they want. But repair cafés aren't only about saving money or protecting the environment. The organisers say that the most important thing is that people learn. Visitors don't just leave their things and come back later. They sit with the volunteer and watch, and often help. Many say they now feel confident enough to do simple repairs at home. There's also tea and homemade cake, so it's a nice way to meet your neighbours. If you have a skill and would like to volunteer, the organisers would love to hear from you.

script.t: So, Kevin, where shall we go in August? I was thinking about Greece. The islands look amazing.
They do, but August is the busiest month there. Everything will be expensive and full of tourists. What about somewhere cooler, like Scotland?
Really? I thought the summer was the perfect time to go to the islands.
Maybe in June or September. In August, you can hardly find a place on the beach.
Scotland? But it rains all the time!
Not all the time. And the landscapes are incredible. We could rent a car and drive around the Highlands, and stay in small guest houses.
Hmm. I'm not a very confident driver, you know. Especially on the left side of the road.
Don't worry, I'll do the driving. And we could spend the first three days in Edinburgh. There's a huge arts festival there in August, with comedy, theatre and music everywhere.
Oh, I've heard about that! My sister went a few years ago and loved it. OK, you're starting to convince me.
Great. The only problem is accommodation in Edinburgh during the festival. We need to book soon.
I'll look tonight. What's our budget?
Let's say no more than a hundred pounds a night for both of us. And if Edinburgh is too expensive, we could stay in a town nearby and take the train in.
Fine. But if it rains every single day, the next holiday is Greece, OK?
Deal.

options: It will be crowded and expensive

script.t: Good evening, everyone. Thank you for coming to this talk. Tonight I'm going to give you some simple advice about sleep, because many of us don't get enough of it. Most adults need between seven and nine hours a night, but surveys show that one in three people sleep less than six. So what can you do? First, try to go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even at the weekend. Your body likes routine. Second, think about your bedroom. It should be dark, quiet and quite cool, about eighteen degrees is ideal. Third, and this is the hardest one for most people, stop looking at screens at least an hour before bed. The light from phones and laptops tells your brain that it's still daytime. Instead, read a paper book or listen to quiet music. Fourth, be careful with coffee. Many people don't realise that caffeine stays in the body for up to ten hours, so a coffee at four in the afternoon can still affect you at midnight. I recommend no coffee after lunch. Finally, if you can't sleep, don't stay in bed worrying. Get up, go to another room and do something relaxing until you feel sleepy. Lying in bed awake teaches your brain that the bed is a place for worrying, not for sleeping. Now, are there any questions?

options: Their light makes your brain think it's day

script.t: You look tired, Paul. Are you OK?
Not really. I haven't slept properly for a week. The new neighbours upstairs are so noisy.
Upstairs? I thought that flat was empty.
It was, but they moved in two weeks ago. They seemed nice when I saw them on the stairs.
Oh no. What kind of noise? Parties?

No, that's the strange thing. They're quite a young couple, and they don't have parties. But every night, around midnight, I hear loud footsteps and something like furniture moving. And then at six in the morning there's music.
Have you spoken to them?
Not yet. I don't want to start a fight. We have to live in the same building for years.

I understand, but they might not know you can hear them. In my old flat, I had the same problem, and when I finally talked to my neighbour, he was really embarrassed. He worked nights in a hospital and had no idea the floor was so thin.
Maybe you're right. What did you do?
I took him some biscuits and introduced myself first, and then I mentioned the noise in a friendly way. He bought some carpets, and the problem was solved.
That's a good idea. I'll knock on their door this weekend. If that doesn't work, I'll write to the building manager.
Good luck. And maybe buy some earplugs in the meantime!

script.t: This week I've been testing the new FitPulse 3 smart watch, which costs one hundred and ninety-nine euros. So, is it worth the money? Let's start with the design. The watch is light and comfortable, and I wore it day and night without any problems. The screen is bright and easy to read, even in strong sunlight. It comes in three colours: black, white and a rather strange orange. For fitness, the FitPulse is excellent. It counts your steps, measures your heart rate and tracks your sleep. I took it running and swimming, and it was very accurate. I particularly liked the reminders. If you sit for more than an hour, it vibrates and tells you to walk around. However, there are some disappointments. The battery only lasts about two days, which is much less than the company promises. And although you can read messages on the watch, you can't reply to them, which I found annoying. The app on the phone is also quite complicated, and it took me twenty minutes to set everything up. So, my opinion? If you mainly want a watch for sport and health, the FitPulse 3 is a great choice. But if you want a watch that does everything your phone does, you should probably spend a little more and choose a different model. I give it seven out of ten.

title: A strange festival
model: Cambridge B1 Preliminary – Listening Part 2/4 (radio feature)

script.t: Every year, on the last Monday in May, hundreds of people gather at the top of a very steep hill in Gloucestershire, in the west of England, for one of the strangest competitions in the world: cheese rolling. The rules are simple. Someone rolls a large, round cheese, weighing about four kilos, down the hill, and a second later, the competitors run after it. The first person to cross the finish line at the bottom wins the cheese. Nobody actually catches it, because it can reach speeds of up to a hundred kilometres an hour! The hill is so steep that most runners fall over and roll down rather than run. Injuries are common, mainly broken arms and legs, and there are always ambulances waiting at the bottom. In 2010, the official event was cancelled because of safety worries, as more than fifteen thousand spectators came. But local people continued to organise it unofficially, and it still happens every year. Nobody knows exactly how old the tradition is, but some historians think it is at least six hundred years old. Today, competitors come from all over the world. In recent years, winners have come from the United States, Canada and Japan. And if you're wondering, for safety reasons the real cheese is now replaced by a lighter foam copy during the race, and the winner receives the real cheese at the end.

script.t: Sara, I didn't know you were vegetarian! When did you stop eating meat?
About six months ago. I watched a documentary about farming and how much water and land are needed to produce meat, and I decided to try it for a month.
And you continued?
Yes. To be honest, I thought it would be much harder. The first two weeks were difficult, I really missed bacon at breakfast! But now I don't think about it.
Don't you get hungry? I always think vegetarian food isn't very filling.
Not at all. I eat a lot of beans, lentils and eggs, and I've learned to cook dishes from India and Mexico, which have amazing vegetarian food. I actually cook much more than before.
What about your family?

My mum was worried at first. She thought I wouldn't get enough iron. So I went to the doctor for a blood test, and everything was fine. Now my mum cooks a vegetarian meal for the whole family every Thursday.
I don't think I could do it. I love burgers too much.
You don't have to stop completely. Why not try one day a week without meat? Lots of people do that.
Hmm, maybe. If you teach me to make one of those Mexican dishes.
Deal! Come round on Saturday.

script.t: Hello, and thank you for registering for this year's City Marathon. Here's some important information for race day, which is Sunday the fourteenth of April. The race starts at half past eight from the main square, but you need to be there by seven forty-five to leave your bags and find your starting area. Your starting area depends on the time you think you'll finish, and it's printed on your race number. Please remember that there will be no parking near the start, so use public transport. The underground will start running two hours earlier than usual on race day, and runners can travel for free if they show their race number. There will be water stations every five kilometres, and energy drinks and bananas at kilometres fifteen, twenty-five and thirty-five. If you feel unwell at any time, stop and speak to one of our medical volunteers, who will be wearing red jackets. At the finish line in the park, you'll receive your medal and a T-shirt. Your family and friends can meet you at the big meeting point next to the lake. Finally, the race closes after six hours. If you're still running at that point, the roads will open again to traffic and you'll need to move onto the pavement. Good luck, and enjoy the day!
